title: Data from Cloud Storage
summary: Data from Cloud Storage describes collection of objects held in managed storage rather than through a normal business application. The targets are object stores such as Amazon S3, Azure Storage and Google Cloud Storage, and the document or file services that sit behind office suites and chat platforms, including OneDrive, Google Drive, Dropbox, Slack, Confluence and Salesforce. Where no front end application exists, the objects are listed and downloaded directly with provider programming interfaces and command line tools, which leaves only provider level access records: data plane read and list calls, storage access logs, anonymous or public requests, and unusual download volume attributed to one identity, key or token. Collection often needs no exploit. Public buckets, broadly shared links, and access granted to every authenticated user are common misconfigurations, and credentials that leak through source repositories or logs are abused just as often as weaknesses in the service itself. Defender differentiation leans on behaviour that legitimate use rarely produces: enumeration of many buckets followed by selective reads, downloads from an unexpected address or client, access by an identity that never uses the console, and copy or archive jobs that move data out of the storage boundary in bulk.

beginner.definition: Cloud storage is space that a provider keeps on the internet for your files and objects. This technique is an attacker reading that space to collect data. They may use stolen keys, a shared link or an open setting on the storage account.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many organisations keep customer records, plans and private documents in cloud storage. A weak setting can expose all of it to anyone on the internet. Copying the data usually leaves no trace on your own computers. The loss is often noticed only after the files appear elsewhere.
howItWorks: The attacker finds a storage account. It may be listed in public code, in a misconfigured setting or from a stolen key.
If the storage is open, no login is needed at all. Anyone who knows the name can list and read the objects.
If a key or token is needed, the attacker uses it with a command line tool or a provider programming interface.
A programming interface is a way for programs to talk to a service. It lets the attacker pull files without opening a web page.
The attacker lists the storage first, then downloads only the objects that look valuable, such as records or backups.
The provider records these reads in its own logs. Your team needs to collect those logs to see what was taken.
beginner.example: Think of a self storage company. Every unit has a door and a lock, but one customer sets their padlock code to blank. Anyone who walks past can open the door, take boxes and close it again. The front office keeps a list of who entered the building, yet nobody reads that list until the customer reports items missing.
takeaways: An open storage setting is an invitation, so check public and shared access on a schedule.
Provider logs are your only witness when data leaves through a storage interface. Keep them and alert on bulk reads.
Treat any leaked key found in code or logs as a possible route into your stored data.

objectives: Explain how object storage is read directly through provider interfaces rather than a business application.
Describe the common misconfigurations that allow cloud storage data to be read without an exploit.
Identify which provider log sources reveal listing and download of stored objects.
Distinguish bulk or unusual storage collection from normal user file access.
State why credentials leaked in code repositories matter to cloud storage security.
